title: Helen Toner Says We Still Can't Trust AI CEOs After Firing
summary: Former OpenAI board member Helen Toner speaks out on AI governance, CEO accountability, and why the industry's trust problem remains unresolved in 2026.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Helen Toner, who voted to remove Sam Altman as OpenAI CEO, argues AI industry leaders remain unaccountable to safety oversight.
- The Georgetown CSET director emphasizes structural governance failures that enable AI CEOs to prioritize growth over responsible deployment.
- Toner's interview highlights ongoing tensions between commercial AI development and the safety frameworks regulators struggle to enforce.


Helen Toner, the former OpenAI board member who participated in[Sam Altman's brief removal as CEO](https://emergent.sh/news/sam-altman-reveals-why-top-openai-talent-left) , has issued a stark warning about the AI industry's accountability crisis. Speaking as executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, Toner argues that structural failures in AI governance continue to enable CEOs to operate without meaningful oversight, despite growing public concerns about safety and transparency.


## The Trust Problem in AI Leadership


Toner's comments come nearly three years after the November 2023 board upheaval that saw Altman temporarily ousted before returning to OpenAI. According to Toner, the fundamental issues that drove that decision remain unresolved across the AI industry. She points to a pattern where commercial pressures consistently override safety considerations, with executives wielding disproportionate influence over technical deployment decisions.


The AI safety researcher emphasizes that current governance structures lack the teeth to hold CEOs accountable when their decisions conflict with public interest. This dynamic plays out repeatedly as companies race to deploy increasingly powerful models without adequate external review or regulatory constraint.


## Why Governance Frameworks Keep Failing


Toner identifies several systemic weaknesses in how AI companies structure oversight. Board members often lack technical expertise to challenge executive claims about model capabilities or risks. Investor pressure to maintain growth trajectories creates incentives to minimize safety concerns. Meanwhile, the absence of binding regulatory frameworks means voluntary commitments remain unenforceable.


These gaps become critical as AI systems take on higher-stakes roles in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure. Toner argues that the industry's self-regulatory approach has demonstrably failed to protect against deployment of undertested or poorly understood systems.


## Policy Implications for 2026 and Beyond


As director of CSET, Toner works directly with policymakers crafting AI regulation. She advocates for mandatory third-party audits, enforceable safety standards, and governance structures that give independent voices real authority over deployment decisions. Her position reflects growing consensus among AI safety researchers that voluntary industry initiatives cannot substitute for regulatory oversight.


The timing of Toner's interview coincides with renewed legislative efforts in the US and EU to establish binding AI safety requirements. Her insider perspective on OpenAI's governance breakdown lends weight to arguments for stronger external controls on AI development.


## Release Details and Context


The interview was officially released on November 14, 2026, as part of The Verge's series examining AI's real-world impacts. Toner's willingness to speak publicly about her OpenAI experience marks a rare instance of board-level transparency in an industry known for opacity around internal decision-making.


## What This Means


Toner's comments signal that the AI governance debate has moved beyond abstract risk scenarios to concrete questions about power, accountability, and who controls technology that increasingly shapes society. Her call for structural reform challenges the industry's preferred narrative of responsible self-governance, arguing instead that external oversight remains essential to align AI development with public safety. For organizations building on AI platforms, her warning underscores the importance of understanding not just technical capabilities but the governance failures that may compromise system reliability and safety.
